passages.t: Sennacherib comes, and the envoy stands at the upper pool
passages.happening:
‘In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah’ (verse 1).

The king of Assyria sends the Rabshakeh with a great army from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. ‘And he stopped by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field’ (verse 2).

Eliakim son of Hilkiah the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe and Joah son of Asaph the recorder go out to meet him (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
For thirty-five chapters Isaiah has warned Judah not to trust in Egypt and promised that the LORD would defend Jerusalem from Assyria. Now the crisis arrives as a story. Chapters 36 to 39 are the only long prose narrative in the book, and they are a hinge. Chapters 36 and 37 tell how Jerusalem was delivered from Assyria, the climax of the book's first half. Chapters 38 and 39 point ahead to the exile addressed in chapters 40 to 66.

These chapters closely parallel 2 Kings 18 to 20, largely word for word. Isaiah leaves out the verses in Kings where Hezekiah admits his rebellion and pays a heavy tribute, and only Isaiah includes Hezekiah's psalm in chapter 38. Most scholars think Isaiah's version was adapted from Kings or from a source both used; some argue the material began with Isaiah's circle.

The campaign is one of the best documented events of the Old Testament period. Sennacherib, king of Assyria from 705 to 681 BC, marched west in 701 BC to crush the revolt Hezekiah had joined. His own annals claim he captured forty-six of Hezekiah's walled cities, shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage, and received a large tribute, but they do not claim that Jerusalem fell. Lachish, Judah's second city, fell after a siege that Sennacherib carved in stone reliefs in his palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum, and archaeologists have excavated the Assyrian siege ramp there.

The envoy stands exactly where Isaiah once met King Ahaz in chapter 7. A generation later, Ahaz's son faces the test his father failed.
passages.later: Kings tells the same story: ‘In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah’ (2 Kings 18:13). Isaiah had once met Ahaz ‘at the end of the aqueduct that feeds the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer’s Field’ (Isaiah 7:3).
passages.hard:
Verse 1 puts the invasion in Hezekiah's fourteenth year. How does that fit the other dates?

If Hezekiah's fourteenth year was 701 BC, he began to reign about 715 BC. But Kings places the fall of Samaria in 722 BC in his sixth year, which would put his accession about 727 BC. Proposed solutions include a period when Hezekiah reigned alongside his father, a copying error in one of the numbers, or different ways of counting a king's years. The site's guide to the kings follows Thiele's reckoning, 716 or 715 to 687 or 686 BC, and sets Galil's 726 to 697 beside it. The date of the invasion itself, 701 BC, is secure from Assyria's own records.
passages.asks: The envoy stood where Ahaz had once refused to trust God. Ask whether there is a place in your life where you failed a test before and now face it again. And ask what it would look like to choose differently this time.

passages.t: In whom are you now trusting?
passages.happening:
The Rabshakeh speaks for ‘the great king, the king of Assyria’ (verse 4): what is the basis of their confidence? Their talk of strategy and strength is empty. ‘In whom are you now trusting, that you have rebelled against me?’ (verse 5).

‘Look now, you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it’ (verse 6). And if they say they trust in the LORD their God, is he not the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed (verse 7)?

He mocks them: he will give them two thousand horses, if they can find riders for them (verse 8). How can they stand against even a minor officer, depending on Egypt for chariots (verse 9)? And finally he claims that the LORD himself told him to go up against this land and destroy it (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The Rabshakeh, a title for a high Assyrian officer, not a personal name, is a skilled propagandist. His speech touches every sore point. Egypt is useless, as Isaiah himself had said. The LORD is offended by Hezekiah's reforms. Judah has no cavalry. And God is on Assyria's side.

His argument about the altars is shrewd. Hezekiah had shut down the local shrines and centralized worship at the Jerusalem temple, and many ordinary people may have resented losing their local places of worship. To an outsider, destroying a god's altars looked like an insult to the god. The biblical writers see it the other way: Kings praises the reform as faithfulness to the LORD.

The question of verse 5, In whom are you now trusting, is the book's own question put in the enemy's mouth. The first hearers would have recognized it.
passages.later: Kings praises Hezekiah: ‘Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel’ (2 Kings 18:5). Isaiah had called Egypt ‘Rahab Who Sits Still’ (Isaiah 30:7).
passages.hard:
Was the Rabshakeh right that Hezekiah had offended the LORD by removing the high places and altars (verse 7)?

The Rabshakeh's argument is clever propaganda. Hezekiah's reform had closed the local shrines and centralized worship in Jerusalem, and from an outsider's point of view that looked like an insult to the god. The envoy uses that suspicion to split the people from their king.

The biblical writers see it the other way. Kings praises Hezekiah for the reform as an act of faithfulness to the LORD, who had commanded that sacrifice be offered only at the place he chose. Modern historians debate how far the reform reached and how archaeology reflects it; the dismantled altar at the shrine of Arad has been connected by some with Hezekiah and dated differently by others. What the chapter shows is the enemy's tactic: twisting obedience into a reason for doubt.
passages.asks: The envoy asked, In whom are you now trusting? Ask how you would answer that honestly today. And ask where a voice is twisting your obedience to God into a reason to doubt him.

passages.t: Shouting in Hebrew to the people on the wall
passages.happening:
Eliakim, Shebna and Joah ask the Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic, which they understand, not in Hebrew where the people on the wall can hear (verse 11). He refuses. His message is for the men on the wall too, who will soon be starving with them in a siege (verse 12).

Then he stands and shouts in Hebrew: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!” (verse 13). Do not let Hezekiah deceive them; he cannot save them (verse 14). Do not let him persuade them to trust in the LORD (verse 15). Make peace with Assyria and come out, and each will eat from his own vine and fig tree and drink from his own cistern (verse 16), until the king comes and takes them away to a land like their own, a land of grain and wine (verse 17).

‘Has the god of any nation ever delivered his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?’ (verse 18). Where are the gods of Hamath, Arpad and Sepharvaim? Did they save Samaria (verse 19)? How then can the LORD save Jerusalem (verse 20)?

‘But the people remained silent and did not answer a word’ (verse 21), for Hezekiah had commanded them not to answer. The officials come to Hezekiah with their clothes torn (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Aramaic was the language of international diplomacy, understood by officials but not by ordinary people. Hebrew was the people's own tongue. The Rabshakeh deliberately speaks in Hebrew so that the soldiers on the wall will hear and lose heart.

His offer is a picture of deportation dressed up as a reward. Assyria moved conquered peoples to new lands, and he promises them a land like their own. The first hearers knew what had happened to Samaria's people two decades earlier.

His boast puts the LORD on the same level as the gods of the cities Assyria had already taken. That is his great mistake, and the next chapter turns on it. The people answer with silence, as their king commanded. Torn clothes were a sign of grief and distress.
passages.later: Kings tells the same scene in nearly the same words (2 Kings 18:26-37). And the psalm of trust sings, ‘Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God’ (Psalm 20:7).
passages.asks: The people stayed silent and did not argue with the voice from outside the wall. Ask what taunting voices you answer that you would do better to bring to God. And ask what offers of comfort in your life are really a kind of exile.
